title: Week 5 · Lesson 15: Pulmonary Pathophysiology — FNP-Level Approach
html:
PHASE 1 · ADVANCED PATHOPHYSIOLOGY + CLINICAL REASONING

Week 5 — Lesson 15: Pulmonary Pathophysiology

FNP-level goal

Approach dyspnea as a safety and physiology problem: identify whether airflow, alveoli, perfusion, pump function, oxygen carrying capacity, or the airway is failing; build a focused differential; and recognize when outpatient evaluation is unsafe.

Learning Objectives

  • Differentiate asthma, COPD, pneumonia, pulmonary embolism (PE), heart failure, and ACS as causes of dyspnea.
  • Connect airway obstruction, alveolar inflammation, V/Q mismatch, shunt, and dead space to hypoxemia.
  • Recognize FNP-level red flags for severe asthma, COPD exacerbation, pneumonia/sepsis, PE, and acute pulmonary edema.
  • Use history, vital signs, exam, ECG, imaging, and probability-based testing appropriately.
  • Choose outpatient care, expedited assessment, or emergency transfer based on stability and risk.

Part 1 — Dyspnea is a diagnostic problem before it is a diagnosis

Shortness of breath can arise from the airway, alveoli, pulmonary vasculature, heart, blood, metabolic state, neuromuscular system, or anxiety—but anxiety is never a safe default before dangerous causes are considered. Begin with airway, breathing, circulation, mental status, oxygenation, respiratory rate, work of breathing, hemodynamics, and time course.

Ask: Is onset sudden or gradual? Is there wheeze, cough, fever, pleuritic pain, chest pressure, orthopnea, hemoptysis, leg swelling, immobility, tobacco exposure, or known cardiac/pulmonary disease? The history changes pretest probability before any test is ordered.

Part 2 — Gas exchange refresher: V/Q mismatch, shunt, and dead space

Effective gas exchange requires ventilation and perfusion to be matched. Low V/Q regions receive blood but too little air, as can occur with asthma, COPD, pneumonia, or pulmonary edema. A shunt is an extreme low-V/Q state in which perfusion reaches poorly ventilated or nonventilated alveoli. Dead space is ventilation without adequate perfusion; PE is the classic clinical example.

Hypoxemia is a sign, not a diagnosis. Explain it by asking whether oxygen is failing to enter the alveoli, diffuse across the membrane, match to perfusion, or be delivered by circulation and hemoglobin.

Part 3 — Asthma: variable airway obstruction

Asthma involves airway inflammation, bronchial hyperresponsiveness, and variable expiratory airflow limitation. Trigger exposure can cause bronchial smooth-muscle constriction, mucosal edema, and mucus production. The patient may report episodic wheeze, cough, chest tightness, or dyspnea that varies over time and with triggers.

Severe asthma is not defined by wheeze volume alone. A patient who is drowsy, confused, exhausted, unable to speak comfortably, hypoxemic, or has a quiet/silent chest may have critically limited airflow and needs immediate emergency-level care. Assess severity with symptoms, work of breathing, respiratory rate, pulse, oxygen saturation, and lung function when feasible; do not delay transfer in an unstable patient.

Part 4 — COPD: persistent airflow limitation with exacerbations

COPD is characterized by persistent respiratory symptoms and airflow limitation, often associated with exposure to noxious particles or gases. Emphysematous destruction reduces alveolar surface area and elastic recoil; chronic bronchitic processes increase mucus and airway inflammation. Exacerbations are acute worsening beyond the patient’s baseline and may be triggered by infection, pollutants, heart failure, PE, pneumothorax, or medication factors.

Do not label every increased cough or dyspnea in a patient with COPD as “just a COPD flare.” Check severity, oxygenation, respiratory rate, mental status, hemodynamics, new chest pain, fever, volume status, and competing diagnoses. Hypercapnia, acidosis, altered mental status, marked hypoxemia, or failure to respond to initial care require urgent escalation.

Part 5 — Pneumonia: alveolar infection and consolidation

Pneumonia is infection of the lung parenchyma. Inflammatory exudate fills alveoli, increasing diffusion distance and creating low-V/Q or shunt-like physiology. Common features include cough, fever/chills, pleuritic chest pain, dyspnea, fatigue, tachypnea, and hypoxemia, but older adults may present with confusion or functional decline rather than classic fever.

FNP reasoning includes illness severity, oxygenation, respiratory effort, hemodynamics, mental status, comorbidities, aspiration risk, and ability to maintain oral intake/follow-up. Hypotension, confusion, escalating oxygen requirement, respiratory distress, or signs of sepsis require emergency evaluation.

Part 6 — Pulmonary embolism: perfusion failure

PE usually results from venous thromboembolism that travels to the pulmonary arterial circulation. Obstructed perfusion creates dead-space ventilation and can increase pulmonary vascular resistance, straining the right ventricle. Presentation may include sudden dyspnea, pleuritic chest pain, tachycardia, syncope, hemoptysis, or hypoxemia, but no single symptom rules PE in or out.

Start with clinical probability and risk factors: prior VTE, recent surgery or immobility, active cancer, estrogen exposure, pregnancy/postpartum status, and signs of DVT. D-dimer is useful for exclusion only in appropriately selected low/intermediate-probability patients; a positive result is nonspecific. High concern, instability, syncope, hypotension, or severe hypoxemia warrants emergency evaluation rather than serial outpatient testing.

Part 7 — Cardiac dyspnea must remain in the differential

Heart failure can cause pulmonary venous congestion and edema; ACS can produce dyspnea with or without classic chest pain; atrial fibrillation and other arrhythmias can reduce filling or output. Orthopnea, paroxysmal nocturnal dyspnea, edema, JVP elevation, crackles, weight gain, exertional pressure, diaphoresis, and an irregular pulse are clues—but none should be interpreted alone.

The lesson is integration: a wheeze does not exclude heart failure, and dyspnea does not exclude ACS or PE. In a high-risk patient, avoid anchoring on a familiar diagnosis.

Part 8 — Focused physical examination

Observe appearance first: posture, speech, accessory-muscle use, cyanosis, diaphoresis, and fatigue. Then assess vital signs, oxygen saturation, lung sounds, symmetry of breath sounds, wheeze, crackles, heart rhythm, perfusion, JVP, edema, calf asymmetry/tenderness, and signs of infection. A normal lung examination does not reliably exclude PE, early pneumonia, or cardiac disease.

Part 9 — Diagnostics should answer a question

Pulse oximetry, ECG, chest imaging, laboratory studies, viral testing, spirometry (when stable), and echocardiography can be valuable, but the order depends on the clinical question. ECG helps assess ischemia and arrhythmia; chest imaging may identify infiltrate, edema, pneumothorax, or another process. In suspected PE, use validated probability assessment and an appropriate D-dimer/imaging strategy rather than ordering D-dimer indiscriminately.

Do not let a reassuring single test override dangerous physiology. A patient with severe work of breathing, hypotension, confusion, or worsening hypoxemia needs emergency stabilization and evaluation.

Case 1 — Severe asthma red flags

A 24-year-old with asthma is speaking one word at a time, appears exhausted, and has a quiet chest. Reduced audible wheeze is not reassuring: extremely low airflow may produce a silent chest. This is severe asthma and requires immediate emergency-level care.

Case 2 — COPD versus heart failure

A 70-year-old with COPD has increased dyspnea, orthopnea, new leg edema, crackles, and weight gain. Do not assume an isolated COPD exacerbation. The pattern also supports possible acute heart-failure congestion, requiring cardiac and volume assessment while considering pulmonary causes.

Case 3 — Sudden dyspnea after immobility

A patient develops sudden dyspnea and pleuritic chest pain after recent surgery and prolonged immobility. The mechanism may be venous thrombus → pulmonary arterial obstruction → dead-space ventilation and RV strain. PE must be evaluated urgently according to clinical probability and stability.

FNP High-Yield Framework

  1. Stabilize first: airway, breathing, circulation, mental status, oxygenation, and work of breathing.
  2. Classify the likely physiology: airway obstruction, alveolar disease, perfusion failure, congestion, ischemia/arrhythmia, or another cause.
  3. Use onset, triggers, risk factors, and exam to create a ranked differential.
  4. Order targeted tests that answer a clinical question and account for pretest probability.
  5. Reassess response and trajectory; worsening physiology overrides an initially familiar label.
  6. Escalate immediately for instability, severe respiratory distress, hypoxemia, altered mentation, shock, syncope, or concerning chest pain.

High-Yield Summary

Asthma: variable airway inflammation/bronchoconstriction; silent chest, exhaustion, confusion, or hypoxemia are emergencies.
COPD: persistent airflow limitation; consider infection, HF, PE, pneumothorax, and hypercapnic failure during worsening symptoms.
Pneumonia: alveolar infection/exudate → low V/Q or shunt physiology; assess severity and sepsis risk.
PE: perfusion obstruction → dead space and possible RV strain; use pretest probability before D-dimer/imaging.
Acute dyspnea: keep HF, ACS, arrhythmia, PE, and pulmonary disease in the differential.
Disposition: severe work of breathing, hypoxemia, instability, confusion, syncope, or concerning chest symptoms require emergency care.
